about: The experience interview's questions. 'core' runs for every thin role, in order, skipping any whose 'covered' pattern already matches the role's evidence; each family adds what hiring managers in that field look for. Sources: Topgrading's chronological interview (Smart), Lou Adler's most-significant-accomplishment probes, Laszlo Bock's 'X relative to Y by doing Z', resume writers' accomplishment questions (Jazvac; PARWCC), NACE Job Outlook 2025, McKinsey's resume advice.

core.ask: What were you hired to do there, and what would 'great' have looked like after a year? Who did you report to?
core.why: Hiring managers judge results against the job's goal (Topgrading's first question about every role).
core.covered: \b(hired to|responsible for|my remit|reporting to|reported to|owned|in charge of)\b

core.ask: How big was it? Team size, budget, customers or accounts, territory, users, volume a week: whatever applies.
core.why: Scope is the first thing a reader uses to place your level.

core.ask: What's the one thing from this role you're proudest of? Walk me through it: the situation, what you did yourself, and what changed because of it.
core.why: Lou Adler's core question: one accomplishment, probed in depth, predicts more than a list of duties.

core.ask: How do you know it worked? A number before and after, against target, or against what others on the team got.
core.why: Bock's formula: accomplished X, relative to Y. A number with a comparison is what a reader trusts.

core.ask: Why were you the one who did it? Were you picked, did you volunteer, or did you spot it yourself?
core.why: Initiative is a top-five attribute employers look for (NACE 2025: at least 70% of employers).

core.ask: What did you start or change that wasn't there before you arrived?
core.why: Resume writers' best question for finding achievements people forget to mention.

core.ask: What would have happened if you hadn't been there?
core.why: Separates what you did from what the team would have done anyway.

core.ask: Any promotion, award, ranking, praise in a review, or a message from a client or your boss that stuck with you?
core.why: Third-party proof: reviews and recognition are evidence a reader believes (and you can quote them).

core.ask: What was the hardest problem or the low point, and what did you do about it?
core.why: Topgrading asks about low points in every role; interviewers will too, so it's worth having the story.

core.ask: If I rang your manager there, what would they say you were best at, and one thing you were working on?
core.why: Topgrading's reference check: your answer should match what a reference would say.

core.ask: Who did you work with or win over: other teams, senior people, clients? Did you train or lead anyone?
core.why: Teamwork is the second thing employers look for (NACE 2025: nearly 80%); leadership is what McKinsey's recruiters look for first.

core.ask: What tools, systems or methods did you use most days?
core.why: These are the words search software matches in your CV.
Every interviewer asks; a short, positive answer prepared now saves a stumble later.
core.covered: \b(left to|moved on|why i left|contract ended|made redundant|role ended)\b

asks: What was your quota or target, and what did you hit? As a percentage, and where that put you on the team.
What was a typical deal: size, how long from first call to signed, and who you sold to (their title)?
How much pipeline did you create yourself: meetings booked a week or month, and how many turned into deals?
New customers or growing existing ones? Which segment: small businesses, mid-market or enterprise?
Tell me about your biggest win: how you found it, what nearly lost it, and how you closed it.
Which partners or deals did you bring in, and what were they worth (revenue, volume or reach)?
Walk me through one negotiation: what each side wanted and where it landed.
Did you open a new market, product line or channel? What came of it?
How big was your book: accounts and their total value?
What were retention, renewals or churn like on your accounts, and against what target?
Any upsell or expansion you drove? Any scores (NPS, CSAT) or faster onboarding?
Which process did you fix or build? What did it take before and after (time, cost, errors)?
What did you run day to day, and at what volume?
Which project had the most moving parts: budget, timeline, teams involved, and did it land on time?
What was the client's problem, and which piece of it was yours?
What did you recommend, was it adopted, and what changed for the client?
How did you work it out: the analysis, the data, and who you presented it to (how senior)?
What did you ship, for whom, and what problem did it solve for them?
Which number moved because of it (adoption, conversion, retention, revenue, time saved)?
How did you decide what to build: research, data, a trade-off you made, and who you had to align?
Which channels or campaigns did you own, and with what budget?
What did they produce: leads, pipeline, sign-ups, revenue, or cost per result, against what before?
Which experiment taught you the most, and what did you change because of it?
Which question did your analysis answer, and what decision changed because of it?
How much data, which tools, and how accurate or fast was the result?
Who used your dashboards or models, and how often?
Which deals, transactions or portfolios did you work on: size, sector and your role in each?
Which models or analyses did you build yourself, and what were they used for?
What did you own end to end (a memo, a forecast, a close, an audit area), and what came of it?
What did you build, and at what scale (users, requests, data)?
What got faster, cheaper or more reliable because of your work, and by how much?
Which part of the stack was yours, and did you review code, mentor or lead anyone?
Which project best shows your work, and can it be shown (a link or case study)?
What research did you do, and what did you change because of it?
What happened after launch: usage, conversion, fewer support tickets?
How many hires or programmes, for which teams, and how fast?
What improved because of you: time to hire, retention, offer acceptance, engagement scores?
What did you build, and who paid for it: customers, revenue, users, funding?
What did you do yourself (selling, building, hiring), and who did you hire?
What would you do differently, and what did it teach you that an employer gets?
How many hours a week, and did your responsibility grow while you were there?
Tell me about one problem you solved there, start to finish.
Did you lead, organise or train anyone, even informally?
